The Hitch, Lavinia exilicauda, is a cyprinid fish endemic to the Sacramento–San Joaquin river system in California. Neonates emerge from demersal, adhesive eggs following an incubation period during which the developing yolk-dependent embryo draws upon endogenous resources. The newly hatched yolk-sac larva is minute, with a wet weight at birth of approximately 0.0012 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0012 grams], reflecting the small egg diameter typical of this lineage. Following yolk-sac resorption, the prolarva transitions to first exogenous feeding, initiating a period of rapid somatic growth. Field surveys indicate that individuals ultimately attain a total length of 36 centimeters [Li = 36 centimeters], a dimension that constitutes the maximum recorded body size for the species. This ultimate length is reached after several years of sustained feeding and is rarely observed across most of the species' range, where environmental conditions often truncate growth before this asymptotic size is realized.

At the onset of gonadal maturation, female Hitch typically achieve reproductive viability once they reach a total length of 20 centimeters [Lp = 20 centimeters]. This length threshold is a reliable indicator of the transition from the immature post-metamorphic juvenile stage to a sexually mature adult capable of vitellogenesis and spawning. Correspondingly, the wet weight at puberty for a female of this size is approximately 46.4 grams [Wwp = approximately 46.4 grams], a mass that reflects the allocation of somatic resources necessary to support oocyte development. Most individuals attain this body weight during their second or third growing season, depending on local thermal regimes and food availability. The relationship between length and mass conforms to a power function typical of the family, providing a robust basis for estimating maturity status from length-frequency distributions in field samples.

Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a constant water temperature of 16 °C [T = 16 °C], the reproductive output of Hitch has been quantified at two distinct body sizes, providing insight into how fecundity scales with length. At a standard length of 21.2 centimeters, gravid females produce approximately 9000 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 9000 eggs per year], a rate that reflects the modest reproductive capacity of medium-sized individuals within the population, equivalent to a reproductive rate at SL 21.2 cm of approximately 24.66 eggs per day  at a temperature of 16 °C [T = 16 °C]. At a standard length of 31.2 centimeters, the annual fecundity increases substantially to roughly 63000 eggs per year [Ri = roughly 63000 eggs per year], demonstrating a steep allometric scaling of reproductive output with body size, corresponding to a reproductive rate at SL 31.2 cm of approximately 172.6 eggs per day  at a temperature of 16 °C [T = 16 °C]. These values were recorded under identical thermal conditions, confirming that temperature alone cannot account for the nearly sevenfold increase in egg production. Such data are critical for parameterizing stock-recruitment models and for understanding the species' compensatory capacity in the face of environmental variability.

The maximum wet weight attained by adult Hitch has been recorded at 292 grams [Wwi = 292 grams], a value derived from the length-weight relationship established for the Sacramento–San Joaquin stock. This ultimate wet weight is achieved only by the oldest and largest individuals, typically those exceeding 30 centimeters in total length. In contrast to the relatively modest 46.4 grams [Wwp = 46.4 grams] at puberty, which signals the onset of reproductive capability, the ultimate wet weight represents the physiological ceiling for somatic growth under ideal conditions. The sixfold increase in mass between puberty and asymptotic size underscores the protracted growth trajectory that characterizes this species. Comparative data from congeneric taxa suggest that such a scaling pattern is associated with an iteroparous, multiple-spawning life history, wherein energy is partitioned between continued somatic investment and repeated reproductive bouts across successive seasons.

The lifespan of Hitch under field conditions has been estimated at approximately 2000 days [am = approximately 2000 days] at a water temperature of 16 °C at a temperature of 16 °C [T = 16 °C]. This longevity corresponds to roughly five and a half years, placing the species among the longer-lived members of its assemblage within the Central Valley. Mortality rates are highest during the larval phase, particularly around the point of no return when yolk reserves are exhausted and exogenous feeding must commence. For those individuals that survive the exotrophic transition and progress through the juvenile stage, the risk of natural mortality declines steadily. Senescence in older adults is marked by a gradual decline in reproductive condition and a heightened vulnerability to physiological stress during the warm summer months. The estimated maximum lifespan provides a key parameter for demographic models and for evaluating the species' resilience to anthropogenic disturbances such as flow alteration and habitat fragmentation.
